I suppose He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named taught him a few tricks!” Black started to laugh, a horrible, mirthless laugh that filled the whole room. “Voldemort, teach me tricks?” he said. Pettigrew flinched as though Black had brandished a whip at him. “What, scared to hear your old master’s name?” said Black. “I don’t blame you, Peter. His lot aren’t very happy with you, are they?” “Don’t know what you mean, Sirius —” muttered Pettigrew, his breathing faster than ever. His whole face was shining with sweat now. “You haven’t been hiding from me for twelve years,” said Black. “You’ve been hiding from Voldemort’s old supporters. I heard things in Azkaban, Peter. . . . They all think you’re dead, or you’d have to answer to them. . . . I’ve heard them screaming all sorts of things in their sleep. Sounds like they think the double-crosser double-crossed them.
detailed_summary: In a tense confrontation, Sirius Black taunts Peter Pettigrew about having been tracked and about the consequences of betraying Voldemort. Pettigrew protests and flinches under Black’s furious mockery, sweating and insisting he doesn’t understand. Black ridicules the idea that Voldemort would teach him harmless ‘tricks,’ and accuses Peter of hiding not from Black but from Voldemort’s former supporters, implying they believe Peter is dead and would punish him if they knew he lived. Lupin questions how anyone could have escaped Azkaban, expressing incredulity that Pettigrew predicted Sirius’s return. Pettigrew, terrified and shrill, suggests Black has Dark powers, while Black jeers that Peter should fear his old master’s followers more. The scene centers on accusation, fear, and revelation: Black’s dominance and contempt, Pettigrew’s panic and denial, and others’ bewilderment at a supposed escape from Azkaban. The exchange reveals distrust, loyalty conflicts, and the fragile position Pettigrew occupies between powerful enemies and former allies.

scene_title: Threat of Voldemort’s Followers and Pettigrew’s Fear
scene_content: I heard things in Azkaban, Peter. . . . They all think you’re dead, or you’d have to answer to them. . . . I’ve heard them screaming all sorts of things in their sleep. Sounds like they think the double-crosser double-crossed them. Voldemort went to the Potters’ on your information . . . and Voldemort met his downfall there.
detailed_summary: In this short scene a character addresses Peter Pettigrew (referred to as Peter) and recounts what has been heard in Azkaban. The speaker reports that the prisoners there believe Peter is dead and, if he were alive, they would hold him accountable — their nightmares are full of accusations and screams suggesting betrayal and a double-cross. The speaker explains that Voldemort attacked the Potter home because of information provided by Peter, and that Voldemort ultimately met his downfall at the Potters' house. The tone is accusatory and ominous: the narrator relays rumors and vivid sleep-screams heard in Azkaban as evidence that the imprisoned souls believe they were betrayed. The passage ties Peter directly to Voldemort’s assault on the Potters, framing him as the informer whose actions led to Voldemort’s attempt on the Potters and subsequent defeat. The scene is focused on revelation and condemnation rather than action, conveying fear, guilt, and the weight of testimony against Peter.

scene_content: And not all Voldemort’s supporters ended up in Azkaban, did they? There are still plenty out here, biding their time, pretending they’ve seen the error of their ways. . . . If they ever got wind that you were still alive, Peter —” “Don’t know . . . what you’re talking about . . . ,” said Pettigrew again, more shrilly than ever. He wiped his face on his sleeve and looked up at Lupin. “You don’t believe this — this madness, Remus —” “I must admit, Peter, I have difficulty in understanding why an innocent man would want to spend twelve years as a rat,” said Lupin evenly. “Innocent, but scared!” squealed Pettigrew. “If Voldemort’s supporters were after me, it was because I put one of their best men in Azkaban — the spy, Sirius Black!” Black’s face contorted. “How dare you,” he growled, sounding suddenly like the bear-sized dog he had been. “I, a spy for Voldemort? When did I ever sneak around people who were stronger and more powerful than myself? But you, Peter — I’ll never understand why I didn’t see you were the spy from the start. You always liked big friends who’d look after you, didn’t you? It used to be us . . . me and Remus . . . and James. . . .” Pettigrew wiped his face again; he was almost panting for breath. “Me, a spy . . . must be out of your mind . . . never . . . don’t know how you can say such a —” “Lily and James only made you Secret-Keeper because I suggested it,” Black hissed, so venomously that Pettigrew took a step backward. “I thought it was the perfect plan . . . a bluff. . . . Voldemort would be sure to come after me, would never dream they’d use a weak, talentless thing like you. . . . It must have been the finest moment of your miserable life, telling Voldemort you could hand him the Potters.” Pettigrew was muttering distractedly; Harry caught words like “far-fetched” and “lunacy,” but he couldn’t help paying more attention to the ashen color of Pettigrew’s face and the way his eyes continued to dart toward the windows and door. “Professor Lupin?” said Hermione timidly. “Can — can I say something?” “Certainly, Hermione,” said Lupin courteously. “Well — Scabbers — I mean, this — this man — he’s been sleeping in Harry’s dormitory for three years. If he’s working for You-Know-Who, how come he never tried to hurt Harry before now?” “There!” said Pettigrew shrilly, pointing at Ron with his maimed hand. “Thank you! You see, Remus? I have never hurt a hair of Harry’s head! Why should I?” “I’ll tell you why,” said Black. “Because you never did anything for anyone unless you could see what was in it for you. Voldemort’s been in hiding for twelve years, they say he’s half dead. You weren’t about to commit murder right under Albus Dumbledore’s nose, for a wreck of a wizard who’d lost all of his power, were you? You’d want to be quite sure he was the biggest bully in the playground before you went back to him, wouldn’t you? Why else did you find a wizard family to take you in? Keeping an ear out for news, weren’t you, Peter? Just in case your old protector regained strength, and it was safe to rejoin him. . . .”
detailed_summary: In this tense scene Remus Lupin, Sirius Black and Peter Pettigrew face one another as accusations about past betrayal are aired. Pettigrew shrieks denials while nervously wiping his face and darting glances toward the windows and door, clearly terrified. Lupin questions the logic of an "innocent man" choosing to spend twelve years as a rat, speaking evenly and calmly. Pettigrew insists he is innocent but scared, claiming he only acted to save himself because Voldemort’s supporters supposedly hunted him. Sirius erupts with furious indignation, calling Pettigrew a liar and reminding him that he, Sirius, would never have been a spy for Voldemort; his tone becomes growling and venomous as he lists how he and the Marauders protected one another and how he engineered James and Lily’s use of Pettigrew as Secret-Keeper as a bluff. Hermione timidly intervenes with a pointed question about why Scabbers — who has slept in Harry’s dormitory for years — never harmed Harry if he were truly loyal to Voldemort, prompting Pettigrew to point at Ron and squeal that he never hurt Harry. Sirius answers with a cold, reasoned accusation that Pettigrew only ever helped himself, waiting for Voldemort to regain strength before returning, and that Pettigrew sought out a wizarding family to eavesdrop for news. The scene ends with Pettigrew muttering and the three others holding firm in their suspicion and anger.

scene_content: “You know what this means?” Sirius said abruptly to Harry as they made their slow progress along the tunnel. “Turning Pettigrew in?” “You’re free,” said Harry. “Yes . . . ,” said Sirius. “But I’m also — I don’t know if anyone ever told you — I’m your godfather.” “Yeah, I knew that,” said Harry. “Well . . . your parents appointed me your guardian,” said Sirius stiffly. “If anything happened to them . . .” Harry waited. Did Sirius mean what he thought he meant? “I’ll understand, of course, if you want to stay with your aunt and uncle,” said Sirius. “But . . . well . . . think about it. Once my name’s cleared . . . if you wanted a . . . a different home . . .” Some sort of explosion took place in the pit
detailed_summary: As Sirius and Harry move slowly through a tunnel, Sirius abruptly asks Harry if he understands what the situation means — specifically mentioning turning Pettigrew in. Harry responds simply, telling Sirius that he is free. Sirius then reveals, haltingly and with visible emotion, that he is Harry's godfather and that Harry's parents had appointed him as guardian should anything have happened to them. He awkwardly offers Harry a choice: he will understand if Harry wants to stay with his aunt and uncle, but suggests that once his name is cleared and if Harry wanted a different home, Harry should think about it. Sirius speaks stiffly and tentatively, clearly nervous about imposing. Harry waits, trying to interpret Sirius's meaning, when some unspecified explosive sound occurs in the pit, interrupting the moment. The scene focuses on the emotional exchange about guardianship, freedom, and the possibility of a new home, highlighting Sirius's vulnerability and Harry's cautious receptiveness.

scene_title: Harry Asks About Moving In; Sirius's Reaction
scene_content: Did Sirius mean what he thought he meant? “I’ll understand, of course, if you want to stay with your aunt and uncle,” said Sirius. “But . . . well . . . think about it. Once my name’s cleared . . . if you wanted a . . . a different home . . .” Some sort of explosion took place in the pit of Harry’s stomach. “What — live with you?” he said, accidentally cracking his head on a bit of rock protruding from the ceiling. “Leave the Dursleys?” “Of course, I thought you wouldn’t want to,” said Sirius quickly. “I understand, I just thought I’d —” “Are you insane?” said Harry, his voice easily as croaky as Sirius’s. “Of course I want to leave the Dursleys! Have you got a house? When can I move in?” Sirius turned right around to look at him; Snape’s head was scraping the ceiling but Sirius didn’t
detailed_summary: In this cramped, tense scene underground, Sirius Black awkwardly offers Harry a possible new home once his name is cleared. Sirius speaks gently and tentatively, trying not to pressure Harry: “I’ll understand, of course, if you want to stay with your aunt and uncle,” then trailing, suggesting Harry could live with him. Harry experiences a visceral emotional reaction — "Some sort of explosion took place in the pit of Harry’s stomach" — and blurts out after cracking his head on rock, surprised and incredulous: “What — live with you?” He immediately follows with blunt enthusiasm, calling Sirius insane when Sirius thinks Harry might prefer the Dursleys, and asking eagerly about moving in: “Of course I want to leave the Dursleys! Have you got a house? When can I move in?” Sirius turns to look at Harry, shocked and relieved; Snape’s presence is implied overhead, scraping the ceiling, adding urgency and danger to the exchange. The scene emphasizes Harry’s longing to escape the Dursleys, Sirius’s cautious hope and tentative offer, and the sudden, raw bond forming between them amid peril.

scene_content: Ron was chained to Pettigrew and Lupin. He leapt forward but Sirius caught him around the chest and threw him back. “Leave it to me — RUN!” There was a terrible snarling noise. Lupin’s head was lengthening. So was his body. His shoulders were hunching. Hair was sprouting visibly on his face and hands, which were curling into clawed paws. Crookshanks’s hair was on end again; he was backing away — As the werewolf reared, snapping its long jaws, Sirius disappeared from Harry’s side.
detailed_summary: Harry, Ron and Hermione are in the thick of a violent confrontation. Ron is physically chained to Peter Pettigrew and Remus Lupin; when he lunges forward Sirius Black catches him by the chest and hurls him backwards while shouting for them to run. A terrible snarling noise fills the air as Lupin begins to transform: his head and body lengthen, shoulders hunch, and hair sprouts visibly on his face and hands, which curl into clawed paws. Crookshanks reacts with fur on end and backs away. As the werewolf rears and snaps its long jaws, Sirius, who had been near Harry, suddenly disappears from Harry’s side. The scene is chaotic, dangerous and swift — transformation, warning, and an abrupt vanishing occur almost together, leaving the trio reeling and forced to act quickly.

scene_content: He had transformed. The enormous, bearlike dog bounded forward. As the werewolf wrenched itself free of the manacle binding it, the dog seized it about the neck and pulled it backward, away from Ron and Pettigrew.
detailed_summary: A gigantic, bearlike dog suddenly appears after a human figure completes a transformation. The enormous dog bounds forward with powerful momentum. As a werewolf struggles against a manacle that had been binding it, the dog grabs the werewolf by the neck and pulls it backward, away from Ron Weasley and Peter Pettigrew. The dog’s intervention separates the dangerous creature from Ron and Pettigrew, physically dragging the werewolf out of immediate reach. There is no spoken dialogue in the supplied lines; the passage focuses on rapid physical action and the sudden presence of a protective or aggressive animal that alters the immediate threat dynamic. The scene implies an abrupt rescue or attack that changes who is endangered and who is safe, leaving Ron and Pettigrew removed from the werewolf’s immediate grasp as the dog exerts control over the transformed figure.

scene_content: They were locked, jaw to jaw, claws ripping at each other — Harry stood, transfixed by the sight, too intent upon the battle to notice anything else. It was Hermione’s scream that alerted him — Pettigrew had dived for Lupin’s dropped wand.
detailed_summary: Harry stands frozen, riveted by a brutal, close-quarters fight: two creatures locked jaw to jaw, claws tearing at one another. He is so absorbed by the violence that he fails to notice other details until Hermione’s scream slices through his stupor. Her cry draws his attention to a new, urgent threat — Peter Pettigrew has lunged for Remus Lupin’s fallen wand. The scene shifts from passive observation to immediate peril as Pettigrew attempts to seize a weapon while the combatants remain entangled. The brief passage contains no spoken dialogue beyond Hermione’s scream, but the actions communicate escalating danger and the potential turning point where possession of a wand could change the outcome. Harry’s trance-like watchfulness, Hermione’s alarm, and Pettigrew’s opportunistic movement toward the wand are the key elements: a frozen witness, a warning signal, and a sudden grab that could alter the balance of the fight.

scene_content: Ron, unsteady on his bandaged leg, fell. There was a bang, a burst of light — and Ron lay motionless on the ground. Another bang — Crookshanks flew into the air and back to the earth in a heap. “Expelliarmus!” Harry yelled, pointing his own wand at Pettigrew; Lupin’s wand flew high into the air and out of sight. “Stay where you are!” Harry shouted, running forward. Too late. Pettigrew had transformed. Harry saw his bald tail whip through the manacle on Ron’s outstretched arm and heard a scurrying through the grass. There was a howl and a rumbling growl; Harry turned to see the werewolf taking flight; it was galloping into the forest — “Sirius, he’s gone, Pettigrew transformed!” Harry yelled.
detailed_summary: Ron, injured and unstable on a bandaged leg, collapses after a sudden bang and burst of light, lying motionless. A second flash sends Crookshanks flying to the ground. Harry reacts instantly: he shouts "Expelliarmus!" and aims his wand at Pettigrew, disarming Lupin as Lupin's wand soars up and out of sight. Harry orders Pettigrew and runs forward, but Pettigrew transforms too quickly — Harry sees Pettigrew's bald tail whip through the manacle on Ron's outstretched arm and hears rapid scurrying through the grass. As the werewolf howls and growls, it flees at speed into the forest. Harry calls out in alarm, identifying the transformation and naming Sirius while reporting Pettigrew's change: "Sirius, he’s gone, Pettigrew transformed!" The scene is frantic and chaotic: spells, transformation, and a hurried retreat into the woods after a violent, confusing confrontation.

scene_content: Shocking business . . . shocking . . . miracle none of them died . . . never heard the like . . . by thunder, it was lucky you were there, Snape. . . .” “Thank you, Minister.” “Order of Merlin, Second Class, I’d say. First Class, if I can wangle it!” “Thank you very much indeed, Minister.” “Nasty cut you’ve got there. . . . Black’s work, I suppose?” “As a matter of fact, it was Potter, Weasley, and Granger, Minister. . . .” “No!” “Black had bewitched them, I saw it immediately. A Confundus Charm, to judge by their behavior. They seemed to think there was a possibility he was innocent. They weren’t responsible for their actions. On the other hand, their interference might have permitted Black to escape. . . . They obviously thought they were going to catch Black single-handed. They’ve got away with a great deal before now. . . . I’m afraid it’s given them a rather high opinion of themselves . . . and of course Potter has always been allowed an extraordinary amount of license by the headmaster —” “Ah, well, Snape . . . Harry Potter, you know . . . we’ve all got a bit of a blind spot where he’s concerned.” “And yet — is it good for him to be given so much special treatment? Personally, I try and treat him like any other student. And any other student would be suspended — at the very least — for leading his friends into such danger. Consider, Minister — against all school rules — after all the precautions put in place for his protection — out-of-bounds, at night, consorting with a werewolf and a murderer — and I have reason to believe he has been visiting Hogsmeade illegally too —” “Well, well . . . we shall see, Snape, we shall see. . . . The boy has undoubtedly been foolish. . . .” Harry lay listening with his eyes tight shut. He felt very groggy. The words he was hearing seemed to be traveling very slowly from his ears to his brain, so that it was difficult to understand. . . . His limbs felt like lead; his eyelids too heavy to lift. . . . He wanted to lie here, on this comfortable bed, forever. . . . “What amazes me most is the behavior of the dementors . . . you’ve really no idea what made them retreat, Snape?” “No, Minister . . . by the time I had come ’round they were heading back to their positions at the entrances. . . .” “Extraordinary. And yet Black, and Harry, and the girl —” “All unconscious by the time I reached them. I bound and gagged Black, naturally, conjured stretchers, and brought them all straight back to the castle.” There was a pause. Harry’s brain seemed to be moving a little faster, and as it did, a gnawing sensation grew in the pit of his stomach. . . . He opened his eyes. Everything was slightly blurred. Somebody had removed his glasses. He was lying in the dark hospital wing. At the very end of the ward, he could make out Madam Pomfrey with her back to him, bending over a bed. Harry squinted. Ron’s red hair was visible beneath Madam Pomfrey’s arm. Harry moved his head over on the pillow. In the bed to his right lay Hermione. Moonlight was falling across her bed. Her eyes were open too. She looked petrified, and when she saw that Harry was awake, pressed a finger to her lips, then pointed to the hospital wing door. It was ajar, and the voices of Cornelius Fudge and Snape were coming through it from the corridor outside. Madam Pomfrey now came walking briskly up the dark ward to Harry’s bed. He turned to look at her. She was carrying the largest block of chocolate he had ever seen in his life. It looked like a small boulder. “Ah, you’re awake!” she said briskly. She placed the chocolate on Harry’s bedside table and began breaking it apart with a small hammer. “How’s Ron?” said Harry and Hermione together. “He’ll live,” said Madam Pomfrey grimly. “As for you two . . . you’ll be staying here until I’m satisfied you’re — Potter, what do you think you’re doing?” Harry was sitting up, putting his glasses back on, and picking up his wand. “I need to see the headmaster,” he said. “Potter,” said Madam Pomfrey soothingly, “it’s all right. They’ve got Black.
detailed_summary: After a dangerous encounter in the forest, Cornelius Fudge and Severus Snape converse outside the hospital wing about the incident: how Black was apparently responsible, how Harry, Ron, and Hermione were found unconscious, and how the dementors behaved oddly. Snape explains he found the trio apparently bewitched (a Confundus Charm), that Black had been bound and gagged, and that the students’ interference may have allowed Black to escape. Fudge praises Snape and jokes about awarding him an Order of Merlin while questioning Dumbledore’s indulgence of Harry. Harry slowly regains consciousness in the hospital wing, groggy and disoriented with his glasses removed. He recognizes Ron and Hermione in nearby beds; Hermione signals him to be quiet and points to the ajar door where Fudge and Snape are speaking. Madam Pomfrey approaches carrying an enormous block of chocolate, breaks pieces with a hammer, and reassures them that Ron will live. Harry tries to get up and demands to see Dumbledore, but Madam Pomfrey gently stops him, telling him that Sirius Black has been secured. The scene emphasizes aftermath, authority scrutiny, and the students’ fragile state.

scene_content:
He’s locked away upstairs. The dementors will be performing the Kiss any moment now —” “WHAT?”

“In here!” Hermione seized Harry’s arm and dragged him across the hall to the door of a broom closet; she opened it, pushed him inside among the buckets and mops, then slammed the door behind them. “What — how — Hermione, what happened?” “We’ve gone back in time,” Hermione whispered, lifting the chain off Harry’s neck in the darkness. “Three hours back . . .” Harry found his own leg and gave it a very hard pinch. It hurt a lot, which seemed to rule out the possibility that he was having a very bizarre dream. “But —” “Shh! Listen! Someone’s coming! I think — I think it might be us!” Hermione had her ear pressed against the cupboard door. “Footsteps across the hall . . . yes, I think it’s us going down to Hagrid’s!” “Are you telling me,” Harry whispered, “that we’re here in this cupboard and we’re out there too?” “Yes,” said Hermione, her ear still glued to the cupboard door. “I’m sure it’s us. It doesn’t sound like more than three people . . . and we’re walking slowly because we’re under the Invisibility Cloak —” She broke off, still listening intently. “We’ve gone down the front steps. . . .” Hermione sat down on an upturned bucket, looking desperately anxious, but Harry wanted a few questions answered. “Where did you get that hourglass thing?” “It’s called a Time-Turner,” Hermione whispered, “and I got it from Professor McGonagall on our first day back. I’ve been using it all year to get to all my lessons. Professor McGonagall made me swear I wouldn’t tell anyone. She had to write all sorts of letters to the Ministry of Magic so I could have one. She had to tell them that I was a model student, and that I’d never, ever use it for anything except my studies. . . . I’ve been turning it back so I could do hours over again, that’s how I’ve been doing several lessons at once, see? But . . . “Harry, I don’t understand what Dumbledore wants us to do. Why did he tell us to go back three hours? How’s that going to help Sirius?” Harry stared at her shadowy face. “There must be something that happened around now he wants us to change,” he said slowly. “What happened? We were walking down to Hagrid’s three hours ago. . . .” “This is three hours ago, and we are walking down to Hagrid’s,” said Hermione. “We just heard ourselves leaving. . . .” Harry frowned; he felt as though he were screwing up his whole brain in concentration. “Dumbledore just said — just said we could save more than one innocent life. . . .” And then it hit him. “Hermione, we’re going to save Buckbeak!” “But — how will that help Sirius?” “Dumbledore said — he just told us where the window is — the window of Flitwick’s office! Where they’ve got Sirius locked up! We’ve got to fly Buckbeak up to the window and rescue Sirius! Sirius can escape on Buckbeak — they can escape together!” From what Harry could see of Hermione’s face, she looked terrified. “If we manage that without being seen, it’ll be a miracle!” “Well, we’ve got to try, haven’t we?” said Harry. He stood up and pressed his ear against the door. “Doesn’t sound like anyone’s there. . . . Come on, let’s go. . . .”

“If anyone’s looking out of the window —” Hermione squeaked, looking up at the castle behind them. “We’ll run for it,” said Harry determinedly. “Straight into the forest, all right? We’ll have to hide behind a tree or something and keep a lookout —” “Okay, but we’ll go around by the greenhouses!” said Hermione breathlessly. “We need to keep out of sight of Hagrid’s front door, or we’ll see us! We must be nearly at Hagrid’s by now!” Still working out what she meant, Harry set off at a sprint, Hermione behind him. They tore across the vegetable gardens to the greenhouses, paused for a moment behind them, then set off again, fast as they could, skirting around the Whomping Willow, tearing toward the shelter of the forest. . . . Safe in the shadows of the trees, Harry turned around; seconds later, Hermione arrived beside him, panting. “Right,” she gasped. “We need to sneak over to Hagrid’s. . . . Keep out of sight, Harry. . . .” They made their way silently through the trees, keeping to the very edge of the forest. Then, as they glimpsed the front of Hagrid’s house, they heard a knock upon his door. They moved quickly behind a wide oak trunk and peered out from either side. Hagrid had appeared in his doorway, shaking and white, looking around to see who had knocked. And Harry heard his own voice. “It’s us. We’re wearing the Invisibility Cloak. Let us in and we can take it off.”

“Yeh shouldn’ve come!” Hagrid whispered. He stood back, then shut the door quickly. “This is the weirdest thing we’ve ever done,” Harry said fervently. “Let’s move along a bit,” Hermione whispered. “We need to get nearer to Buckbeak!” They crept through the trees until they saw the nervous hippogriff, tethered to the fence around Hagrid’s pumpkin patch. “Now?” Harry whispered. “No!” said Hermione. “If we steal him now, those Committee people will think Hagrid set him free! We’ve got to wait until they’ve seen he’s tied outside!” “That’s going to give us about sixty seconds,” said Harry. This was starting to seem impossible. At that moment, there was a crash of breaking china from inside Hagrid’s cabin. “That’s Hagrid breaking the milk jug,” Hermione whispered. “I’m going to find Scabbers in a moment —” Sure enough, a few minutes later, they heard Hermione’s shriek of surprise. “Hermione,” said Harry suddenly, “what if we — we just run in there and grab Pettigrew —” “No!” said Hermione in a terrified whisper. “Don’t you understand? We’re breaking one of the most important Wizarding laws! Nobody’s supposed to change time, nobody! You heard Dumbledore, if we’re seen —” “We’d only be seen by ourselves and Hagrid!” “Harry, what do you think you’d do if you saw yourself bursting into Hagrid’s house?” said Hermione. “I’d — I’d think I’d gone mad,” said Harry, “or I’d think there was some Dark Magic going on —” “Exactly! You wouldn’t understand, you might even attack yourself! Don’t you see? Professor McGonagall told me what awful things have happened when wizards have meddled with time. . . .
detailed_summary: Hermione and Harry, having used a Time-Turner, realize they have gone back three hours and hide in a broom closet as their earlier selves approach. Hermione explains she received the Time-Turner from Professor McGonagall and has been using it to attend multiple lessons; they overhear their past selves walking toward Hagrid’s. Realizing Dumbledore intends them to change events, Harry deduces they must rescue Sirius by flying Buckbeak to the window of Flitwick’s office so Sirius can escape. They sneak through the grounds, skirt the Whomping Willow, and hide in the forest to observe Hagrid’s cottage. They hear their own voices at Hagrid’s door and watch Hagrid bring Buckbeak out, tethered near the pumpkin patch. Hermione warns against stealing Buckbeak before the Committee members see him; she also resists taking direct action like grabbing Pettigrew, reminding Harry of the dangers of meddling with time and the warnings McGonagall gave about awful consequences. The scene ends with urgency, fear, and careful planning as they prepare to attempt a risky rescue without being seen.

scene_content:
Loads of them ended up killing their past or future selves by mistake!” “Okay!” said Harry. “It was just an idea, I just thought —” But Hermione nudged him and pointed toward the castle. Harry moved his head a few inches to get a clear view of the distant front doors. Dumbledore, Fudge, the old Committee member, and Macnair the executioner were coming down the steps. “We’re about to come out!” Hermione breathed.

The Patronus turned. It was cantering back toward Harry across the still surface of the water. It wasn’t a horse. It wasn’t a unicorn, either. It was a stag. It was shining brightly as the moon above . . . it was coming back to him. . . . It stopped on the bank. Its hooves made no mark on the soft ground as it stared at Harry with its large, silver eyes. Slowly, it bowed its antlered head. And Harry realized . . . “Prongs,” he whispered. But as his trembling fingertips stretched toward the creature, it vanished. Harry stood there, hand still outstretched. Then, with a great leap of his heart, he heard hooves behind him — he whirled around and saw Hermione dashing toward him, dragging Buckbeak behind her. “What did you do?” she said fiercely. “You said you were only going to keep a lookout!” “I just saved all our lives . . . ,” said Harry. “Get behind here — behind this bush — I’ll explain.” Hermione listened to what had just happened with her mouth open yet again. “Did anyone see you?” “Yes, haven’t you been listening? I saw me but I thought I was my dad! It’s okay!” “Harry, I can’t believe it. . . . You conjured up a Patronus that drove away all those dementors! That’s very, very advanced magic. . . .” “I knew I could do it this time,” said Harry, “because I’d already done it. . . . Does that make sense?”

“Harry, I can’t believe it. . . . You conjured up a Patronus that drove away all those dementors! That’s very, very advanced magic. . . .” “I knew I could do it this time,” said Harry, “because I’d already done it. . . . Does that make sense?” “I don’t know — Harry, look at Snape!” Together they peered around the bush at the other bank. Snape had regained consciousness. He was conjuring stretchers and lifting the limp forms of Harry, Hermione, and Black onto them. A fourth stretcher, no doubt bearing Ron, was already floating at his side. Then, wand held out in front of him, he moved them away toward the castle. “Right, it’s nearly time,” said Hermione tensely, looking at her watch. “We’ve got about forty-five minutes until Dumbledore locks the door to the hospital wing. We’ve got to rescue Sirius and get back into the ward before anybody realizes we’re missing. . . .” They waited, watching the moving clouds reflected in the lake, while the bush next to them whispered in the breeze. Buckbeak, bored, was ferreting for worms again. “D’you reckon he’s up there yet?” said Harry, checking his watch. He looked up at the castle and began counting the windows to the right of the West Tower. “Look!” Hermione whispered. “Who’s that? Someone’s coming back out of the castle!” Harry stared through the darkness. The man was hurrying across the grounds, toward one of the entrances. Something shiny glinted in his belt. “Macnair!” said Harry. “The executioner! He’s gone to get the dementors! This is it, Hermione —”

“Whoa!” he said, pulling backward as hard as he could. Buckbeak slowed down and they found themselves at a stop, unless you counted the fact that they kept rising up and down several feet as the hippogriff beat his wings to remain airborne. “He’s there!” Harry said, spotting Sirius as they rose up beside the window. He reached out, and as Buckbeak’s wings fell, was able to tap sharply on the glass. Black looked up. Harry saw his jaw drop. He leapt from his chair, hurried to the window, and tried to open it, but it was locked. “Stand back!” Hermione called to him, and she took out her wand, still gripping the back of Harry’s robes with her left hand. “Alohomora!” The window sprang open. “How — how — ?” said Black weakly, staring at the hippogriff. “Get on — there’s not much time,” said Harry, gripping Buckbeak firmly on either side of his sleek neck to hold him steady. “You’ve got to get out of here — the dementors are coming — Macnair’s gone to get them.” Black placed a hand on either side of the window frame and heaved his head and shoulders out of it. It was very lucky he was so thin. In seconds, he had managed to fling one leg over Buckbeak’s back and pull himself onto the hippogriff behind Hermione. “Okay, Buckbeak, up!” said Harry, shaking the rope. “Up to the tower — come on!”
detailed_summary: Harry, Hermione, and Buckbeak hide near the lake while watching Dumbledore, Fudge, an old committee member, and Macnair leave the castle. A shining stag Patronus appears, bows to Harry, and vanishes, prompting Harry to recognize it as "Prongs." Hermione rushes over dragging Buckbeak; she scolds Harry for not keeping watch, while Harry insists he saved them by producing the Patronus. They watch Snape revive and carry unconscious bodies—including presumably Ron—into the castle on stretchers. Hermione checks the time: they have about forty-five minutes before the hospital wing is locked and they must rescue Sirius. Macnair leaves to fetch dementors. Later, atop Buckbeak, Harry taps at a tower window to alert Sirius; Hermione unlocks it with Alohomora. Harry warns Sirius that dementors are coming and Macnair has gone to fetch them. Sirius climbs out the window with difficulty and jumps onto Buckbeak behind Hermione. Harry urges Buckbeak to fly up to the tower so they can escape with Sirius before the dementors arrive.

scene_content: Harry clenched his teeth. He caught a glimpse of Snape’s smirk as he and Fudge passed Harry and Hermione’s hiding place. Their footsteps died away. Harry and Hermione waited a few moments to make sure they’d really gone, then started to run in the opposite direction. Down one staircase, then another, along a new corridor — then they heard a cackling ahead. “Peeves!” Harry muttered, grabbing Hermione’s wrist. “In here!” They tore into a deserted classroom to their left just in time.
detailed_summary: Harry and Hermione are hiding as Severus Snape and Cornelius Fudge pass by nearby; Harry notices Snape smirking as they move past. Once the footsteps die away, Harry and Hermione wait a moment to ensure the pair have gone, then sprint off in the opposite direction. They descend two staircases and run along a corridor before hearing a cackling sound ahead — Peeves. Harry mutters the name and seizes Hermione's wrist, urgently steering them into a deserted classroom to evade detection, making it inside just in time. The scene is tense and hurried, emphasizing Harry's alertness to danger, Hermione's presence beside him, and the looming threat represented by adults and the poltergeist. No dialogue beyond Harry's brief mutter occurs, but actions and small reactions (Snape's smirk, the footsteps, the cackling) convey the urgency and relief when they reach temporary safety.

scene_content: Peeves seemed to be bouncing along the corridor in boisterous good spirits, laughing his head off. “Oh, he’s horrible,” whispered Hermione, her ear to the door. “I bet he’s all excited because the dementors are going to finish off Sirius. . . .” She checked her watch. “Three minutes, Harry!”\n\n“Oh, he’s horrible,” whispered Hermione, her ear to the door. “I bet he’s all excited because the dementors are going to finish off Sirius. . . .” She checked her watch. “Three minutes, Harry!” They waited until Peeves’s gloating voice had faded into the distance, then slid back out of the room and broke into a run again. “Hermione — what’ll happen — if we don’t get back inside — before Dumbledore locks the door?” Harry panted. “I don’t want to think about it!” Hermione moaned, checking her watch again. “One minute!” They had reached the end of the corridor with the hospital wing entrance. “Okay — I can hear Dumbledore,” said Hermione tensely. “Come on, Harry!” They crept along the corridor. The door opened. Dumbledore’s back appeared. “I am going to lock you in,” they heard him saying. “It is five minutes to midnight. Miss Granger, three turns should do it. Good luck.” Dumbledore backed out of the room, closed the door, and took out his wand to magically lock it.
detailed_summary: Peeves bounces boisterously along the corridor, gloating as Harry and Hermione eavesdrop nervously behind a door. Hermione, with her ear pressed to the door, whispers that Peeves is "horrible" and suggests he is delighted because the dementors might finish off Sirius. She checks her watch and urges Harry that they have only minutes — "Three minutes, Harry!" They wait until Peeves's voice fades, then slip back into the corridor and run. Harry panics about being locked out and asks Hermione what will happen if they miss getting back inside before Dumbledore locks the door. Hermione, tense and anxious, checks her watch again — "One minute!" — as they hurry toward the hospital wing entrance. Hermione announces she can hear Dumbledore; they creep along and the door opens to reveal Dumbledore’s back. From inside they hear Dumbledore say he is going to lock them in and instruct Miss Granger that "three turns should do it." Dumbledore closes the door and uses his wand to magically lock it. The scene is driven by urgent, whispered exchanges and the ticking clock of approaching midnight, with fear for Sirius and the pressure of returning before the lock takes effect.

scene_content: Panicking, Harry and Hermione ran forward. Dumbledore looked up, and a wide smile appeared under the long silver mustache. “Well?” he said quietly. “We did it!” said Harry breathlessly. “Sirius has gone, on Buckbeak. . . .”\n\nDumbledore beamed at them. “Well done. I think —” He listened intently for any sound within the hospital wing. “Yes, I think you’ve gone too — get inside — I’ll lock you in —” Harry and Hermione slipped back inside the dormitory. It was empty except for Ron, who was still lying motionless in the end bed. As the lock clicked behind them, Harry and Hermione crept back to their own beds, Hermione tucking the Time-Turner back under her robes.
detailed_summary: Panicking, Harry and Hermione rush forward to find Dumbledore in the hospital wing; Dumbledore looks up and smiles, asking "Well?" Harry, out of breath and excited, tells him that Sirius has escaped on Buckbeak. Dumbledore beams approval, listens for sounds in the ward, and tells them to get inside so he can lock the dormitory. Harry and Hermione slip back into the Gryffindor dormitory and find Ron still lying motionless in the far bed. As the lock clicks, they creep back to their own beds, and Hermione tucks the Time-Turner back under her robes. The scene captures relief, quiet triumph, and furtive secrecy: the successful rescue (Sirius on Buckbeak) and the need to hide their actions from others while protecting Ron and themselves. Dialogue is minimal but revealing: Harry’s breathless announcement, Dumbledore’s calm approval and protective instructions, and Hermione’s discrete action with the Time-Turner emphasize quick thinking, teamwork, and the consequences of their time-bending actions.

scene_content: A moment later, Madam Pomfrey came striding back out of her office. “Did I hear the headmaster leaving? Am I allowed to look after my patients now?” She was in a very bad mood. Harry and Hermione thought it best to accept their chocolate quietly. Madam Pomfrey stood over them, making sure they ate it. But Harry could hardly swallow. He and Hermione were waiting, listening, their nerves jangling. . . . And then, as they both took a fourth piece of chocolate from Madam Pomfrey, they heard a distant roar of fury echoing from somewhere above them. . . . “What was that?” said Madam Pomfrey in alarm. Now they could hear angry voices, growing louder and louder. Madam Pomfrey was staring at the door. “Really — they’ll wake everybody up! What do they think they’re doing?” Harry was trying to hear what the voices were saying. They were drawing nearer — “He must have Disapparated, Severus. We should have left somebody in the room with him. When this gets out —” “HE DIDN’T DISAPPARATE!” Snape roared, now very close at hand. “YOU CAN’T APPARATE OR DISAPPARATE INSIDE THIS CASTLE!
detailed_summary: Madam Pomfrey returns from her office in a bad mood and asks if the headmaster has left so she can tend her patients; Harry and Hermione accept chocolate from her while they wait, though Harry finds it hard to swallow because they are anxious and listening. As they take a fourth piece of chocolate, a distant roar of fury echoes from above. Madam Pomfrey alarms, asking what the noise was and fretting that the angry voices will wake everyone. The voices grow louder and nearer; Pomfrey stares at the door, scolding that the noise will wake others. Harry strains to hear the words and recognizes the approaching argument. The voices draw closer and someone suggests that a person must have Disapparated and that someone should have been left in the room with him, warning of consequences. Snape suddenly roars back, very close, denying the claim — emphatically shouting that the person did not Disapparate and reminding them that Apparating or Disapparating inside the castle is impossible. The scene ends amid the rising commotion and outrage, with the ward tense and noisy as the staff confront whatever has occurred above.

scene_content: His face was twisted; spit was flying from his mouth. “Calm down, man!” Fudge barked. “You’re talking nonsense!” “YOU DON’T KNOW POTTER!” shrieked Snape. “HE DID IT, I KNOW HE DID IT —” “That will do, Severus,” said Dumbledore quietly. “Think about what you are saying. This door has been locked since I left the ward ten minutes ago. Madam Pomfrey, have these students left their beds?” “Of course not!” said Madam Pomfrey, bristling. “I would have heard them!” “Well, there you have it, Severus,” said Dumbledore calmly. “Unless you are suggesting that Harry and Hermione are able to be in two places at once, I’m afraid I don’t see any point in troubling them further.” Snape stood there, seething, staring from Fudge, who looked thoroughly shocked at his behavior, to Dumbledore, whose eyes were twinkling behind his glasses. Snape whirled about, robes swishing behind him, and stormed out of the ward. “Fellow seems quite unbalanced,” said Fudge, staring after him. “I’d watch out for him if I were you, Dumbledore.” “Oh, he’s not unbalanced,” said Dumbledore quietly. “He’s just suffered a severe disappointment.” “He’s not the only one!” puffed Fudge. “The Daily Prophet’s going to have a field day! We had Black cornered and he slipped through our fingers yet again! All it needs now is for the story of that hippogriff’s escape to get out, and I’ll be a laughingstock! Well . . .
detailed_summary: In the hospital ward confrontation, Cornelius Fudge angrily accuses and tries to control the situation while Severus Snape erupts, shrieking that Harry did something wrong and insisting "YOU DON'T KNOW POTTER!" and "HE DID IT, I KNOW HE DID IT —". Dumbledore intervenes calmly, asking Snape to think about his words and confirming that the ward door had been locked since he left ten minutes earlier. Madam Pomfrey firmly states the students have not left their beds, undercutting Snape's accusation. Dumbledore points out that, unless Harry and Hermione can be in two places at once, further trouble is unnecessary. Snape, furious and humiliated, storms out of the ward. Fudge remarks that Snape seems unbalanced and warns Dumbledore to watch out for him, but Dumbledore quietly observes that Snape has merely suffered a severe disappointment. Fudge, still worried about his public image, frets about the Daily Prophet and how the escaped hippogriff and Sirius Black’s evasion will make him a laughingstock. The scene closes with Fudge's self-concern about the fallout, while Dumbledore remains measured and lightly amused by Snape’s reaction.

scene_content: Well . . . I’d better go and notify the Ministry. . . .” “And the dementors?” said Dumbledore. “They’ll be removed from the school, I trust?” “Oh yes, they’ll have to go,” said Fudge, running his fingers distractedly through his hair. “Never dreamed they’d attempt to administer the Kiss on an innocent boy. . . . Completely out of control . . . no, I’ll have them packed off back to Azkaban tonight. . . . Perhaps we should think about dragons at the school entrance. . . .” “Hagrid would like that,” said Dumbledore with a swift smile at Harry and Hermione. As he and Fudge left the dormitory, Madam Pomfrey hurried to the door and locked it again.
detailed_summary: In this brief scene Dumbledore and Minister Fudge discuss the aftermath of a dangerous incident involving dementors. Fudge reacts flustered and defensive, promising to notify the Ministry and remove the dementors from Hogwarts; he expresses disbelief that the dementors attempted to administer the Kiss on an innocent boy and suggests sending them back to Azkaban immediately. He also makes a somewhat offhand remark about considering dragons at the school entrance, to which Dumbledore responds with a swift, approving smile mentioning Hagrid’s fondness for dragons. As Dumbledore and Fudge leave the dormitory, Madam Pomfrey quickly locks the door behind them. The dialogue emphasizes Fudge’s anxious, distracted manner and Dumbledore’s calm, mildly amused composure, while the locking of the door by Madam Pomfrey implies a protective, controlling caretaking action following the incident.

scene_content: Why are we in here? Where’s Sirius? Where’s Lupin? What’s going on?” Harry and Hermione looked at each other. “You explain,” said Harry, helping himself to some more chocolate.\n\n“Know I shouldn’ feel happy, after wha’ happened las’ night,” he said. “I mean, Black escapin’ again, an’ everythin’ — but guess what?” “What?” they said, pretending to look curious. “Beaky! He escaped! He’s free! Bin celebratin’ all night!” “That’s wonderful!” said Hermione, giving Ron a reproving look because he looked as though he was close to laughing. “Yeah . . . can’t’ve tied him up properly,” said Hagrid, gazing happily out over the grounds. “I was worried this mornin’, mind . . . thought he mighta met Professor Lupin on the grounds, but Lupin says he never ate anythin’ las’ night. . . .” “What?” said Harry quickly. “Blimey, haven’ yeh heard?” said Hagrid, his smile fading a little.
detailed_summary: Ron wakes up in a room with Harry and Hermione, cheerful despite troubling news from the previous night. Harry asks urgently about Sirius and Lupin, but Ron and Hermione exchange looks and ask Ron to explain. Ron speaks in his familiar West Country-inflected, casual manner, admitting he knows he "shouldn' feel happy" after what happened but blurting out that "Black escapin' again" and that "Beaky! He escaped! He's free! Bin celebratin' all night!" Hermione reacts with a reproving look because Ron seems close to laughing at the news. Hagrid, present and delighted, comments that they "can't've tied him up properly" and that he was worried earlier, thinking Black might have met Professor Lupin on the grounds; Lupin reportedly said he "never ate anythin' las' night." Harry seizes on that detail, asking "What?" in alarm, and Hagrid's smile fades as he says, "Blimey, haven' yeh heard?" The scene conveys a jarring mix of celebration and unease: Ron and Hagrid are elated about Sirius Black's escape, Hermione is disapproving of their amusement, and Harry becomes concerned by Lupin's odd remark about not having eaten, suggesting something important has changed or been discovered.

scene_content: He lowered his voice, even though there was nobody in sight. “Er — Snape told all the Slytherins this mornin’. . . . Thought everyone’d know by now . . . Professor Lupin’s a werewolf, see. An’ he was loose on the grounds las’ night. . . . He’s packin’ now, o’ course.” “He’s packing?” said Harry, alarmed. “Why?” “Leavin’, isn’ he?” said Hagrid, looking surprised that Harry had to ask. “Resigned firs’ thing this mornin’. Says he can’t risk it happenin’ again.” Harry scrambled to his feet. “I’m going to see him,” he said to Ron and Hermione. “But if he’s resigned —” “— doesn’t sound like there’s anything we can do —” “I don’t care. I still want to see him. I’ll meet you back here.”
detailed_summary: Hagrid speaks quietly, though no one else is nearby, and tells Harry, Ron, and Hermione that Snape informed all the Slytherins that morning that Professor Lupin is a werewolf and had been loose on the school grounds the previous night. Hagrid states that Lupin is "packin' now," meaning he is leaving; when Harry questions what "packing" means, Hagrid clarifies that Lupin resigned first thing that morning because he cannot risk another incident. Alarmed, Harry decides he will go see Lupin despite the resignation and tells Ron and Hermione he will meet them back where they are. Ron and Hermione respond practically, noting there may be nothing they can do, but Harry insists he still wants to see Lupin. The scene centers on the revelation of Lupin's condition, his resignation, Hagrid's blunt, colloquial speech, and Harry's immediate emotional response and determination to act.

scene_title: The Dursleys' New Regime and Harry's Hidden Supplies
scene_content: So — after many tantrums, after arguments that shook Harry’s bedroom floor, and many tears from Aunt Petunia — the new regime had begun. The diet sheet that had been sent by the Smeltings school nurse had been taped to the fridge, which had been emptied of all Dudley’s favorite things — fizzy drinks and cakes, chocolate bars and burgers — and filled instead with fruit and vegetables and the sorts of things that Uncle Vernon called “rabbit food.” To make Dudley feel better about it all, Aunt Petunia had insisted that the whole family follow the diet too. She now passed a grapefruit quarter to Harry. He noticed that it was a lot smaller than Dudley’s. Aunt Petunia seemed to feel that the best way to keep up Dudley’s morale was to make sure that he did, at least, get more to eat than Harry. But Aunt Petunia didn’t know what was hidden under the loose floorboard upstairs.
detailed_summary: After many tantrums, arguments and tears from Aunt Petunia, the Dursleys begin a new regime to follow a diet prescribed by the Smeltings school nurse. The diet sheet is taped to the fridge and Vernon empties Dudley’s preferred treats—fizzy drinks, cakes, chocolate bars and burgers—replacing them with fruit, vegetables and what Vernon calls “rabbit food.” Aunt Petunia enforces the diet for the whole family to keep Dudley’s spirits up and passes Harry a quarter of a grapefruit that is noticeably smaller than Dudley’s. The household dynamic is strained and petty: Aunt Petunia deliberately gives Dudley more than Harry to maintain Dudley’s morale. Harry observes these humiliations quietly and is aware that something of his is concealed under the loose floorboard upstairs, which Aunt Petunia does not know about. The scene focuses on domestic cruelty thinly veiled as concern for Dudley, the unequal treatment of Harry, and Harry’s secret resource that contrasts with his mistreatment.

scene_title: Harry's Secret Provisions and Birthday Gifts Arrive
scene_content: She had no idea that Harry was not following the diet at all. The moment he had got wind of the fact that he was expected to survive the summer on carrot sticks, Harry had sent Hedwig to his friends with pleas for help, and they had risen to the occasion magnificently. Hedwig had returned from Hermione’s house with a large box stuffed full of sugar-free snacks. (Hermione’s parents were dentists.) Hagrid, the Hogwarts gamekeeper, had obliged with a sack full of his own homemade rock cakes. (Harry hadn’t touched these; he had had too much experience of Hagrid’s cooking.) Mrs. Weasley, however, had sent the family owl, Errol, with an enormous fruitcake and assorted meat pies. Poor Errol, who was elderly and feeble, had needed a full five days to recover from the journey.
detailed_summary: Summary of Harry's Secret Provisions and Birthday Gifts Arrive

scene_content: And then on Harry’s birthday (which the Dursleys had completely ignored) he had received four superb birthday cakes, one each from Ron, Hermione, Hagrid, and Sirius. Harry still had two of them left, and so, looking forward to a real breakfast when he got back upstairs, he ate his grapefruit without complaint. Uncle Vernon laid aside his paper with a deep sniff of disapproval and looked down at his own grapefruit quarter. “Is this it?” he said grumpily to Aunt Petunia. Aunt Petunia gave him a severe look, and then nodded pointedly at Dudley, who had already finished his own grapefruit quarter and was eyeing Harry’s with a very sour look in his piggy little eyes. Uncle Vernon gave a great sigh, which ruffled his large, bushy mustache, and picked up his spoon.
detailed_summary: On Harry's birthday -- which the Dursleys had ignored -- he had received four excellent birthday cakes from friends: Ron, Hermione, Hagrid, and Sirius. Harry still has two cakes left and, looking forward to a proper breakfast after going back upstairs, eats his grapefruit without complaint. At the breakfast table Uncle Vernon expresses disapproval by laying aside his paper and sniffs deeply, then asks Aunt Petunia grumpily if that is all he gets. Aunt Petunia responds with a severe look and a pointed nod toward Dudley. Dudley, having already finished his own grapefruit quarter, eyes Harry's with a very sour look. Uncle Vernon sighs loudly, which ruffles his large mustache, and picks up his spoon. The scene highlights the contrast between Harry's small pleasures and the Dursleys' disapproving, petty behavior during a moment that should be Harry's birthday morning.

scene_title: Someone at the Door and a Mysterious Letter
scene_content: The doorbell rang. Uncle Vernon heaved himself out of his chair and set off down the hall. Quick as a flash, while his mother was occupied with the kettle, Dudley stole the rest of Uncle Vernon’s grapefruit. Harry heard talking at the door, and someone laughing, and Uncle Vernon answering curtly. Then the front door closed, and the sound of ripping paper came from the hall. Aunt Petunia set the teapot down on the table and looked curiously around to see where Uncle Vernon had got to. She didn’t have to wait long to find out; after about a minute, he was back. He looked livid. “You,” he barked at Harry. “In the living room. Now.” Bewildered, wondering what on earth he was supposed to have done this time, Harry got up and followed Uncle Vernon out of the kitchen and into the next room. Uncle Vernon closed the door sharply behind both of them. “So,” he said, marching over to the fireplace and turning to face Harry as though he were about to pronounce him under arrest. “So.” Harry would have dearly loved to have said, “So what?” but he didn’t feel that Uncle Vernon’s temper should be tested this early in the morning, especially when it was already under severe strain from lack of food. He therefore settled for looking politely puzzled. “This just arrived,” said Uncle Vernon.
detailed_summary: In the kitchen early in the morning, the Dursley household is interrupted by the ringing of the doorbell. Uncle Vernon leaves his chair and goes to the front; while his mother attends the kettle, Dudley quickly steals the rest of Uncle Vernon’s grapefruit. Harry hears voices and laughter at the door, then Uncle Vernon answering curtly. After the front door closes, ripping paper is heard in the hall. Aunt Petunia, having set the teapot down, looks around for Uncle Vernon and soon sees him return looking furious. He angrily orders Harry into the living room. Bewildered and hungry, Harry follows Vernon; the door is shut sharply behind them. Vernon paces to the fireplace, stares at Harry as if about to accuse him, and produces something, announcing, “This just arrived.” The scene ends with Vernon confronting Harry in a tense, accusatory tone about an item that has been delivered to the house.

scene_content: He brandished a piece of purple writing paper at Harry. “A letter. About you.” Harry’s confusion increased. Who would be writing to Uncle Vernon about him? Who did he know who sent letters by the postman? Uncle Vernon glared at Harry, then looked down at the letter and began to read aloud: Dear Mr. and Mrs. Dursley, We have never been introduced, but I am sure you have heard a great deal from Harry about my son Ron.
detailed_summary: At the Dursleys' kitchen table, Uncle Vernon suddenly brandishes a piece of purple writing paper and tells Harry he is holding a letter about him. Harry is confused and wonders who would write to Uncle Vernon concerning him and who he even knows who sends letters by the post. Vernon glares at Harry, then reads the opening of the letter aloud: a formal salutation beginning "Dear Mr. and Mrs. Dursley," followed by a line explaining that the writer and the Dursleys have never been introduced and referencing hearing "a great deal from Harry about my son Ron." The scene centers on the unexpected arrival of written correspondence that directly concerns Harry, Vernon’s puzzlement and guarded hostility, and the revealing first lines of a missive that connects the Dursleys to the writer through Harry and their son Ron. The dialogue is short and edged with curiosity and tension, emphasizing Harry’s bewilderment and Vernon’s brusque, formal delivery as he reads the letter aloud.

scene_title: The Quidditch World Cup Invitation Details
scene_content: As Harry might have told you, the final of the Quidditch World Cup takes place this Monday night, and my husband, Arthur, has just managed to get prime tickets through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports. I do hope you will allow us to take Harry to the match, as this really is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity; Britain hasn’t hosted the Cup for thirty years, and tickets are extremely hard to come by. We would of course be glad to have Harry stay for the remainder of the summer holidays, and to see him safely onto the
detailed_summary: A letter-writer—presumably Mrs. Weasley—explains to Harry that the Quidditch World Cup final is on Monday night and that her husband Arthur has obtained prime tickets through his Department of Magical Games and Sports connections. She asks permission to take Harry to the match, stressing it is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity since Britain hasn't hosted the Cup for thirty years and tickets are extremely scarce. She also offers for Harry to stay with them for the remainder of the summer holidays and promises to see him safely onto whatever follows (the sentence is cut off). The tone is polite, slightly formal, and solicitous; the speaker frames the invitation as both a rare treat and an act of guardianship, emphasizing their connections and care for Harry's welfare. The excerpt contains no direct speech from Harry himself; the entire quoted passage is the letter writer's appeal on Harry's behalf, focusing on logistics (date: Monday night), provenance of tickets (Arthur's Department connections), rarity (once-in-a-lifetime, Britain hasn't hosted for thirty years), and an offer of extended hospitality and supervision for Harry during the holidays.

scene_content: It would be best for Harry to send us your answer as quickly as possible in the normal way, because the Muggle postman has never delivered to our house, and I am not sure he even knows where it is. Hoping to see Harry soon, Yours sincerely, P.S. I do hope we’ve put enough stamps on.
detailed_summary: Summary of Postal Peculiarities and Postman Reaction

scene_content: Other people might not understand why Uncle Vernon was making a fuss about too many stamps, but Harry had lived with the Dursleys too long not to know how touchy they were about anything even slightly out of the ordinary. Their worst fear was that someone would find out that they were connected (however distantly) with people like Mrs Weasley. Uncle Vernon was still glaring at Harry, who tried to keep his expression neutral. If he didn’t do or say anything stupid, he might just be in for the treat of a lifetime. He waited for Uncle Vernon to say something, but he merely continued to glare. Harry decided to break the silence. “So — can I go then?” he asked.
detailed_summary: In this short scene Harry endures Uncle Vernon’s hostile glare as tensions over a trivial matter (too many stamps) simmer. The narrator explains that the Dursleys are hypersensitive to anything slightly out of the ordinary because they fear being linked to people like Mrs Weasley. Uncle Vernon makes no verbal reply; his reaction is purely a sustained, menacing stare directed at Harry. Harry, trained by years with the Dursleys, keeps his face carefully neutral and calculates that saying or doing nothing foolish might earn him a major reward. After waiting for Uncle Vernon to break the silence, Harry decides to speak first and asks, quietly and cautiously, if he can leave: "So — can I go then?" The scene emphasizes Harry’s practiced restraint, the Dursleys’ paranoid social anxieties, and the power of a single charged silence broken by a short, hopeful question from Harry.

scene_content: A slight spasm crossed Uncle Vernon’s large purple face. The mustache bristled. Harry thought he knew what was going on behind the mustache: a furious battle as two of Uncle Vernon’s most fundamental instincts came into conflict. Allowing Harry to go would make Harry happy, something Uncle Vernon had struggled against for thirteen years. On the other hand, allowing Harry to disappear to the Weasleys’ for the rest of the summer would get rid of him two weeks earlier than anyone could have hoped, and Uncle Vernon hated having Harry in the house. To give himself thinking time, it seemed, he looked down at Mrs Weasley’s letter again. “Who is this woman?” he said, staring at the signature with distaste. “You’ve seen her,” said Harry. “She’s my friend Ron’s mother, she was meeting him off the Hog — off the school train at the end of last term.” He had almost said “Hogwarts Express,” and that was a sure way to get his uncle’s temper up.
detailed_summary: Uncle Vernon reacts physically and verbally to a letter from Mrs Weasley, his face flushing purple and his mustache bristling as he fights internally between two instincts: keeping Harry miserable and getting rid of him early. Harry watches and interprets Vernon’s expression and thoughts, recognizing the duel between Vernon’s stubborn desire to deny Harry happiness and his stronger wish to be rid of him. To stall and think, Vernon peers at the signature on the letter and sneers, asking, “Who is this woman?” Harry replies plainly, identifying her as Ron’s mother and noting she had met Ron off the train at the end of term. Harry almost says “Hogwarts Express” but stops himself, knowing the full name will anger his uncle further. The exchange establishes Uncle Vernon’s hostile, petty temperament and Harry’s restrained, factual tone when correcting or informing Vernon, while revealing Harry’s awareness of Vernon’s motives and his desire to avoid provoking a larger outburst.

Other people might not understand why Uncle Vernon was making a fuss about too many stamps, but Harry had lived with the Dursleys too long not to know how touchy they were about anything even slightly out of the ordinary. Their worst fear was that someone would find out that they were connected (however distantly) with people like Mrs. Weasley. Uncle Vernon was still glaring at Harry, who tried to keep his expression neutral. If he didn’t do or say anything stupid, he might just be in for the treat of a lifetime.
detailed_summary: Uncle Vernon is angrily reacting to something involving stamps; he finds the situation funny and is making a fuss over what he perceives as too many stamps. Harry stays silent, carefully controlling his expression and thoughts. He recognizes why the Dursleys are so touchy about anything unusual: their deepest fear is that someone will discover they are connected, however distantly, to people like Mrs. Weasley. Harry understands the stakes from long experience living with them and therefore decides not to provoke Uncle Vernon. He keeps his face neutral and refrains from saying anything stupid, hoping that by staying quiet he might be rewarded — perhaps even receiving an exceptional treat. The passage focuses on Harry’s internal assessment of the Dursleys’ sensitivities and his strategic decision to remain calm under Uncle Vernon’s glare.

scene_title: Harry Asks to Go and Names Sirius
scene_content: He waited for Uncle Vernon to say something, but he merely continued to glare. Harry decided to break the silence. “So — can I go then?” he asked. A slight spasm crossed Uncle Vernon’s large purple face. The mustache bristled. Harry thought he knew what was going on behind the mustache: a furious battle as two of Uncle Vernon’s most fundamental instincts came into conflict. Allowing Harry to go would make Harry happy, something Uncle Vernon had struggled against for thirteen years. On the other hand, allowing Harry to disappear to the Weasleys’ for the rest of the summer would get rid of him two weeks earlier than anyone could have hoped, and Uncle Vernon hated having Harry in the house. To give himself thinking time, it seemed, he looked down at Mrs. Weasley’s letter again. “Who is this woman?” he said, staring at the signature with distaste. “You’ve seen her,” said Harry. “She’s my friend Ron’s mother, she was meeting him off the Hog — off the school train at the end of last term.” He had almost said “Hogwarts Express,” and that was a sure way to get his uncle’s temper up. Nobody ever mentioned the name of Harry’s school aloud in the Dursley household. Uncle Vernon screwed up his enormous face as though trying to remember something very unpleasant. “Dumpy sort of woman?” he growled finally. “Load of children with red hair?” Harry frowned. He thought it was a bit rich of Uncle Vernon to call anyone “dumpy,” when his own son, Dudley, had finally achieved what he’d been threatening to do since the age of three, and become wider than he was tall. Uncle Vernon was perusing the letter again. “Quidditch,” he muttered under his breath. “Quidditch — what is this rubbish?” Harry felt a second stab of annoyance. “It’s a sport,” he said shortly. “Played on broom —” “All right, all right!” said Uncle Vernon loudly. Harry saw, with some satisfaction, that his uncle looked vaguely panicky. Apparently his nerves couldn’t stand the sound of the word “broomsticks” in his living room. He took refuge in perusing the letter again. Harry saw his lips form the words “send us your answer . . . in the normal way.” He scowled. “What does she mean, ‘the normal way’?” he spat. “Normal for us,” said Harry, and before his uncle could stop him, he added, “you know, owl post. That’s what’s normal for wizards.” Uncle Vernon looked as outraged as if Harry had just uttered a disgusting swearword. Shaking with anger, he shot a nervous look through the window, as though expecting to see some of the neighbors with their ears pressed against the glass. “How many times do I have to tell you not to mention that unnaturalness under my roof?” he hissed, his face now a rich plum color. “You stand there, in the clothes Petunia and I have put on your ungrateful back —” “Only after Dudley finished with them,” said Harry coldly, and indeed, he was dressed in a sweatshirt so large for him that he had had to roll back the sleeves five times so as to be able to use his hands, and which fell past the knees of his extremely baggy jeans. “I will not be spoken to like that!” said Uncle Vernon, trembling with rage. But Harry wasn’t going to stand for this. Gone were the days when he had been forced to take every single one of the Dursleys’ stupid rules. He wasn’t following Dudley’s diet, and he wasn’t going to let Uncle Vernon stop him from going to the Quidditch World Cup, not if he could help it. Harry took a deep, steadying breath and then said, “Okay, I can’t see the World Cup. Can I go now, then? Only I’ve got a letter to Sirius I want to finish. You know — my godfather.” He had done it.
detailed_summary: Harry confronts Uncle Vernon after Mrs. Weasley’s letter arrives asking for an answer about Harry attending the Quidditch World Cup. Uncle Vernon glares and fumes, visibly torn between wanting to keep Harry miserable and wanting him gone sooner. Harry answers questions about Mrs. Weasley — identifying her as Ron’s mother who met him at the train — and mentions Quidditch and brooms, which clearly unsettles Vernon. Vernon reacts with outrage when Harry says wizards send letters by owl post and when Harry uses the word 'broomsticks,' treating wizarding matters as obscene. Vernon scowls at the phrase 'send us your answer . . . in the normal way' and insists Harry must not mention 'that unnaturalness' under his roof. Harry, fed up with accepting the Dursleys’ rules and determined not to be stopped from going to the World Cup, asserts himself: he declines to follow Dudley’s diet, refuses Vernon’s insults, and asks again to be allowed to go, adding that he needs to finish a letter to his godfather, Sirius. The confrontation highlights the power dynamics in the Dursley household, Harry’s growing assertiveness, and Vernon’s rigid, fearful hostility toward the wizarding world.

scene_title: Uncle Vernon's Inner Conflict and Reluctant Permission
scene_content: He had said the magic words. Now he watched the purple recede blotchily from Uncle Vernon’s face, making it look like badly mixed black currant ice cream. “You’re — you’re writing to him, are you?” said Uncle Vernon, in a would-be calm voice — but Harry had seen the pupils of his tiny eyes contract with sudden fear. “Well — yeah,” said Harry, casually. “It’s been a while since he heard from me, and, you know, if he doesn’t, he might start thinking something’s wrong.” He stopped there to enjoy the effect of these words. He could almost see the cogs working under Uncle Vernon’s thick, dark, neatly parted hair. If he tried to stop Harry writing to Sirius, Sirius would think Harry was being mistreated.
detailed_summary: Harry speaks to Uncle Vernon after having used persuasive words — implied magical or strongly convincing language — and watches the purple drain from Vernon's face, likening it to badly mixed black currant ice cream. Uncle Vernon attempts a calm voice and asks, “You’re — you’re writing to him, are you?” but his pupils contract with fear, betraying him. Harry answers casually, saying yes, that he is writing to Sirius because it has been a while since Sirius heard from him and Sirius might think something is wrong if he didn’t get a letter. Harry pauses to enjoy the psychological effect of his statement, imagining Vernon’s thoughts working beneath his neatly parted hair. Harry recognizes that if Vernon prevents him writing to Sirius, Sirius might suspect Harry is being mistreated, and he uses that to influence Vernon. The exchange reveals Harry’s calculated calm, Vernon’s thinly veiled fear, and the emotional leverage Harry believes he holds through correspondence with Sirius.

scene_content: If he told Harry he couldn’t go to the Quidditch World Cup, Harry would write and tell Sirius, who would know Harry was being mistreated. There was only one thing for Uncle Vernon to do. Harry could see the conclusion forming in his uncle’s mind as though the great mustached face were transparent.
detailed_summary: In this short scene Harry imagines the consequences if Uncle Vernon forbids him to attend the Quidditch World Cup. Harry considers writing to Sirius because he believes Sirius would understand and recognise if Harry were being mistreated. He watches Uncle Vernon’s thoughts form in his mind, visualising Vernon’s ‘great mustached face’ as though it were transparent, and anticipates that Vernon will reach an obvious, unpleasant conclusion — suggesting Vernon will take a punitive or controlling action. There is no spoken dialogue in the excerpt; the passage conveys Harry’s inner reasoning and his mental image of Vernon plotting. The emotional tone is anxious but practical: Harry quickly calculates a course of action (tell Sirius) and reads his uncle’s intent like a sequence he can predict. The scene establishes Harry’s reliance on Sirius as an ally and shows Uncle Vernon as a domineering, scheming presence even without explicit speech.

scene_content: Harry tried not to smile, to keep his own face as blank as possible. And then — “Well, all right then. You can go to this ruddy . . . this stupid . . . this World Cup thing. You write and tell these — these Weasleys they’re to pick you up, mind. I haven’t got time to go dropping you off all over the country. And you can spend the rest of the summer there. And you can tell your — your godfather . . . tell him . . . tell him you’re going.”
detailed_summary: In this short scene a guardian figure (speaking angrily and reluctantly) tells Harry he may go to the World Cup but orders conditions and expresses frustration about travel arrangements and time. The speaker interrupts themselves with repeated small exclamations and stammers — "this ruddy . . . this stupid . . . this World Cup thing" — then insists the Weasleys must pick Harry up and that the guardian does not have time to drive him around the country. The guardian also tells Harry to inform his godfather that he is allowed to go. Harry attempts to keep a neutral expression, trying not to smile and aiming to keep his face blank while the other person grumbles and gives permission with conditions. The scene is dominated by clipped, exasperated commands and repeated phrases as the guardian yields permission grudgingly; Harry's internal restraint is the only noted emotional reaction from him. No other characters are present, and the dialogue centers on travel logistics, permission, and the guardian's irritation.

scene_content: “They’re late!” he snarled at Harry. “I know,” said Harry. “Maybe — er — the traffic’s bad, or something.” Ten past five . . . then a quarter past five . . . Harry was starting to feel anxious himself now. At half past, he heard Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia conversing in terse mutters in the living room. “No consideration at all.” “We might’ve had an engagement.” “Maybe they think they’ll get invited to dinner if they’re late.” “Well, they most certainly won’t be,” said Uncle Vernon, and Harry heard him stand up and start pacing the living room. “They’ll take the boy and go, there’ll be no hanging around. That’s if they’re coming at all. Probably mistaken the day. I daresay their kind don’t set much store by punctuality. Either that or they drive some tin-pot car that’s broken d — AAAAAAAARRRRRGH!”\n\n“What is it?” gasped Aunt Petunia, who had backed into the wall and was staring, terrified, toward the fire. “What is it, Vernon?” But they were left in doubt barely a second longer. Voices could be heard from inside the blocked fireplace. “Ouch! Fred, no — go back, go back, there’s been some kind of mistake — tell George not to — OUCH! George, no, there’s no room, go back quickly and tell Ron —” “Maybe Harry can hear us, Dad — maybe he’ll be able to let us out —” There was a loud hammering of fists on the boards behind the electric fire. “Harry? Harry, can you hear us?” The Dursleys rounded on Harry like a pair of angry wolverines. “What is this?” growled Uncle Vernon. “What’s going on?” “They — they’ve tried to get here by Floo powder,” said Harry, fighting a mad desire to laugh. “They can travel by fire — only you’ve blocked the fireplace — hang on —” He approached the fireplace and called through the boards. “Mr. Weasley? Can you hear me?” The hammering stopped. Somebody inside the chimney piece said, “Shh!” “Mr. Weasley, it’s Harry . . . the fireplace has been blocked up. You won’t be able to get through there.” “Damn!” said Mr. Weasley’s voice. “What on earth did they want to block up the fireplace for?” “They’ve got an electric fire,” Harry explained. “Really?” said Mr. Weasley’s voice excitedly. “Eclectic, you say? With a plug? Gracious, I must see that. . . . Let’s think . . . ouch, Ron!” Ron’s voice now joined the others’. “What are we doing here? Has something gone wrong?” “Oh no, Ron,” came Fred’s voice, very sarcastically. “No, this is exactly where we wanted to end up.” “Yeah, we’re having the time of our lives here,” said George, whose voice sounded muffled, as though he was squashed against the wall. “Boys, boys . . .” said Mr. Weasley vaguely. “I’m trying to think what to do. . . . Yes . . . only way . . . Stand back, Harry.” Harry retreated to the sofa. Uncle Vernon, however, moved forward. “Wait a moment!” he bellowed at the fire. “What exactly are you going to —” BANG. The electric fire shot across the room as the boarded-up fireplace burst outward, expelling Mr. Weasley, Fred, George, and Ron in a cloud of rubble and loose chippings. Aunt Petunia shrieked and fell backward over the coffee table; Uncle Vernon caught her before she hit the floor, and gaped, speechless, at the Weasleys, all of whom had bright red hair, including Fred and George, who were identical to the last freckle. “That’s better,” panted Mr. Weasley, brushing dust from his long green robes and straightening his glasses. “Ah — you must be Harry’s aunt and uncle!” Tall, thin, and balding, he moved toward Uncle Vernon, his hand outstretched, but Uncle Vernon backed away several paces, dragging Aunt Petunia. Words utterly failed Uncle Vernon. His best suit was covered in white dust, which had settled in his hair and mustache and made him look as though he had just aged thirty years. “Er — yes — sorry about that,” said Mr. Weasley, lowering his hand and looking over his shoulder at the blasted fireplace. “It’s all my fault. It just didn’t occur to me that we wouldn’t be able to get out at the other end. I had your fireplace connected to the Floo Network, you see — just for an afternoon, you know, so we could get Harry. Muggle fireplaces aren’t supposed to be connected, strictly speaking — but I’ve got a useful contact at the Floo Regulation Panel and he fixed it for me. I can put it right in a jiffy, though, don’t worry.
